@@@ USER
How do I create and use a Python virtual environment on Windows, and what do I do when PowerShell says "running scripts is disabled on this system"?
@@@ ASSISTANT
A virtual environment (venv) gives one project its own copy of Python packages, so projects do not break each other.

```powershell
# 1. Create it inside the project folder (once)
python -m venv .venv

# 2. Activate it (the prompt now starts with (.venv))
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

# 3. Install packages into this environment only
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
pip install numpy requests

# 4. Save the exact versions so you can rebuild the environment later
pip freeze > requirements.txt

# 5. Leave the environment
deactivate

# Later, on another machine or after deleting .venv:
python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

**If activation fails with "running scripts is disabled":** Windows blocks PowerShell scripts by default. Allow locally created scripts for your own user only:

```powershell
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned
```

Then run the activate command again. In the old Command Prompt, use `.venv\Scripts\activate.bat`, which has no such restriction.

Tips:
- Add `.venv/` to `.gitignore`. Commit `requirements.txt`, not the environment itself.
- To check you are using the right Python: `Get-Command python` should point inside `.venv`.
- PyTorch with GPU support is installed with the command from pytorch.org (it uses a special download address for the CUDA version), not with a plain `pip install torch`.
- Delete a broken environment by removing the `.venv` folder and creating it again.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
Give me the Cargo commands I will use every day when building a Rust app.
@@@ ASSISTANT
```bash
cargo new myapp            # create a binary project (use --lib for a library)
cd myapp

cargo check                # type-check only: fastest way to see compile errors
cargo build                # debug build (fast to compile, slow to run)
cargo run                  # build and run
cargo run -- --name Asha   # pass arguments to your program (after the --)
cargo build --release      # optimized build in target/release (slow to compile, fast to run)

cargo test                 # run all tests
cargo test parse           # only tests whose name contains "parse"
cargo test -- --nocapture  # show println! output while testing

cargo fmt                  # format the code in the standard style
cargo clippy               # lints: catches common mistakes and non-idiomatic code

cargo add serde            # add a dependency (writes it to Cargo.toml)
cargo add tokio --features full
cargo remove serde         # remove it again
cargo update               # update dependencies within the allowed versions
cargo tree                 # show the dependency tree

cargo doc --open           # build and open documentation for your code and dependencies
cargo clean                # delete the target folder (frees disk space, forces a full rebuild)
```

Good habits:
- While coding, run `cargo check` often. It is much faster than `cargo build` because it skips producing the program.
- Before sharing code: `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy`, `cargo test`.
- Always measure speed with `--release`. A debug build can be 10 to 100 times slower.
- The `target` folder can grow to many gigabytes; keep it out of git (`/target` in `.gitignore`) and out of backups.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
How do I call a web API from the terminal, with a JSON body and a header, on Windows and on Linux/macOS?
@@@ ASSISTANT
In PowerShell use `Invoke-RestMethod`, which also turns JSON replies into objects. Everywhere else use `curl`.

PowerShell:

```powershell
# GET request, reply parsed from JSON
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "https://httpbin.org/get"

# POST with a JSON body and a header
$body = @{ name = "Asha"; age = 30 } | ConvertTo-Json
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "https://httpbin.org/post" -Method Post `
    -Body $body -ContentType "application/json" `
    -Headers @{ Authorization = "Bearer my-token" }

# Only the status code (-SkipHttpErrorCheck needs PowerShell 7 or newer)
(Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "https://httpbin.org/status/404" -SkipHttpErrorCheck).StatusCode
```

Linux, macOS and Git Bash (`curl`):

```bash
curl -s https://httpbin.org/get

curl -s -X POST https://httpbin.org/post \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer my-token" \
  -d '{"name": "Asha", "age": 30}'

curl -i https://httpbin.org/status/404        # -i shows the response headers
curl -L -o page.html https://example.com      # -L follows redirects, -o saves to a file
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://example.com   # print only the status code
```

Notes:
- In Windows PowerShell 5, `curl` is an alias for `Invoke-WebRequest` and does not accept curl options. Type `curl.exe` to run the real curl that ships with Windows 10 and 11.
- Single quotes around the JSON in bash stop the shell from touching the double quotes inside.
- Never paste real tokens into commands you keep in shell history or scripts you share; read them from an environment variable (`$env:TOKEN` in PowerShell, `$TOKEN` in bash).
@@@ END

@@@ USER
How do I zip a folder and back up a project to another drive on Windows from the terminal?
@@@ ASSISTANT
Use `Compress-Archive` for a zip file, and `robocopy` for copying a whole folder tree efficiently.

```powershell
# Zip the contents of a folder
Compress-Archive -Path .\myproject\* -DestinationPath .\myproject-backup.zip -Force

# Unzip it somewhere else
Expand-Archive -Path .\myproject-backup.zip -DestinationPath .\restored

# Copy a folder to another drive, skipping heavy folders.
# /L only LISTS what would happen: run this first!
robocopy C:\Projects\myproject D:\Backup\myproject /E /XD node_modules target .git /L

# Real copy: remove /L. Copy only new and changed files each time.
robocopy C:\Projects\myproject D:\Backup\myproject /E /XD node_modules target .git
```

What the robocopy options mean:
- `/E` copies subfolders, including empty ones.
- `/XD name1 name2` excludes folders with those names.
- `/L` preview only, nothing is copied.
- `/MIR` makes the destination an exact mirror, **including deleting files there that are not in the source**. Use it only when you really want that, and always preview with `/L` first.

Good to know:
- `robocopy` exit codes 0 to 7 mean success (for example 1 = files were copied); 8 or higher means a failure.
- `Compress-Archive` can be slow and has size limits for very large folders. For big backups use `robocopy`, or `tar -a -c -f backup.zip folder`, which comes with modern Windows.
- Exclude `node_modules` and `target` folders: they can be rebuilt and make backups huge.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
Explain redirection and pipes in the terminal: >, >>, 2>&1, and |. How do I save a program's output to a file and also watch it live?
@@@ ASSISTANT
Programs have two output streams: **stdout** (normal output) and **stderr** (errors and warnings). Redirection sends them to files; a pipe sends stdout into another program.

```powershell
python script.py > out.txt            # stdout to a file (overwrite)
python script.py >> out.txt           # stdout appended to the end of the file
python script.py 2> errors.txt        # only the error stream to a file
python script.py > all.txt 2>&1       # both streams into one file
python script.py *> all.txt           # PowerShell shortcut: every stream

# A pipe: output of the left command is the input of the right one
Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5

# Show output on screen AND save it
python script.py 2>&1 | Tee-Object -FilePath run.log

# Watch a log file grow in real time (like tail -f)
Get-Content run.log -Tail 20 -Wait
```

The same ideas in bash:

```bash
python script.py > out.txt 2>&1       # both streams to one file
python script.py 2>&1 | tee run.log   # screen and file together
tail -f run.log                       # follow a growing file
grep -i error run.log | wc -l         # count the lines containing "error"
```

Remember:
- `>` replaces the file; use `>>` if you do not want to lose earlier content.
- The order matters in `> all.txt 2>&1`: first point stdout at the file, then point stderr to the same place.
- Press Ctrl+C to leave `-Wait` / `tail -f`; it does not stop the program that is writing the file.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
Show me a normal git workflow for a feature branch: create it, commit, update from main, merge, and fix a merge conflict.
@@@ ASSISTANT
```bash
# Start from an up-to-date main
git switch main
git pull

# Create the feature branch and work on it
git switch -c feature/dark-mode
git add -A
git commit -m "Add dark mode toggle"

# Keep your branch current with main while you work
git fetch origin
git merge origin/main

# Send it to the remote and open a pull request
git push -u origin feature/dark-mode

# After it is approved: merge into main and clean up
git switch main
git pull
git merge --no-ff feature/dark-mode
git push
git branch -d feature/dark-mode
```

**Fixing a merge conflict.** If two branches changed the same lines, `git merge` stops and marks the file:

```text
<<<<<<< HEAD
timeout = 30
=======
timeout = 60
>>>>>>> origin/main
```

1. Open the file and decide what the correct result is. Everything between `<<<<<<<` and `>>>>>>>` is yours to rewrite. Delete all three marker lines, leaving only the final code (for example `timeout = 60`).
2. Mark it as resolved and finish:

```bash
git add config.txt
git commit          # the merge message is already filled in
```

3. Changed your mind? `git merge --abort` returns to the state before the merge.

Useful extras:
- `git status` always tells you what to do next.
- `git log --oneline --graph --all` draws the branches in the terminal.
- Merge keeps the full history. `git rebase main` makes a straight line instead, but rewrites your commits, so never rebase commits that others have already pulled.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
How do I run a long program (like model training) in the background on Windows, keep its output in a log file, and check on it or stop it?
@@@ ASSISTANT
Use `Start-Process` with output redirection, then follow the log file.

```powershell
# Make sure the log folder exists
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force logs | Out-Null

# Start in the background with no window; output goes to files
Start-Process -FilePath python -ArgumentList "train.py" `
    -RedirectStandardOutput logs\run.log -RedirectStandardError logs\err.log `
    -WindowStyle Hidden

# Watch the log live (Ctrl+C stops watching, not the program)
Get-Content logs\run.log -Tail 20 -Wait

# Is it still running? How much memory does it use?
Get-Process python | Select-Object Id, CPU, @{n = 'RAM_GB'; e = { [math]::Round($_.WorkingSet64 / 1GB, 2) }}

# GPU load, refreshed every 5 seconds
nvidia-smi -l 5

# Stop it
Stop-Process -Name python
```

Important for training programs:
- If your trainer saves checkpoints, stop it the way it expects (for example Ctrl+C in its own window, or a stop script) so that it can save first. `Stop-Process` ends it instantly and you may lose everything since the last save.
- A hidden window means you cannot press Ctrl+C in it. If you want a safe stop, run the program in a normal terminal window instead.
- `-RedirectStandardOutput` and `-RedirectStandardError` must point to different files.
- Laptops: plug in the charger and set the power plan to "High performance", or the GPU will slow down; also disable sleep while training.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
How do I find files by name or by modification date from the terminal?
@@@ ASSISTANT
PowerShell uses `Get-ChildItem` with filters; Linux, macOS and Git Bash use `find`.

PowerShell:

```powershell
# All .log files anywhere below the current folder
Get-ChildItem -Recurse -Filter *.log

# Changed in the last 2 days
Get-ChildItem -Recurse -File | Where-Object { $_.LastWriteTime -gt (Get-Date).AddDays(-2) }

# Bigger than 100 MB
Get-ChildItem -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object { $_.Length -gt 100MB }

# Name contains "report" (any extension), show full path
Get-ChildItem -Recurse -File -Filter "*report*" | Select-Object FullName

# Delete .tmp files: preview first with -WhatIf
Get-ChildItem -Recurse -Filter *.tmp | Remove-Item -WhatIf
```

bash:

```bash
find . -name "*.log"                    # by name
find . -type f -mtime -2                # changed in the last 2 days
find . -type f -size +100M              # bigger than 100 MB
find . -iname "*report*"                # case-insensitive name
find . -name "*.tmp" -type f -delete    # delete (check without -delete first!)
```

Tips:
- `-Filter` in PowerShell is much faster than `-Include`, because the file system does the filtering.
- Before any delete command, run the same command without the delete part (or with `-WhatIf`) and read the list.
- `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` hides "access denied" messages for protected folders.
@@@ END
